title: Choosing an Azure Hosting Model
description: Use a simple decision framework to pick the right Azure compute service for your next project.

data.text: Choosing a hosting model does not have to be complicated. Ask a few questions about your app, and the right service usually becomes obvious. This lesson gives you a practical framework to make that decision confidently.
Start with the workload characteristics, then narrow down to the service that fits best.

rows: Do you need full OS control?
App Service, Functions, or Container Apps
Is cost the top priority and traffic is low?
Do you need the simplest possible deployment?

data.title: Real-World Examples
items: **Marketing website** — App Service. It is always on, cheap, and easy to deploy.
**Invoice PDF generator triggered by an upload** — Functions. A blob trigger starts the function only when a file arrives.
**E-commerce API with a shopping cart** — App Service. Stable, scalable, and supports .NET or Node.
**Scheduled nightly data cleanup job** — Functions with a timer trigger. Runs automatically at the scheduled time.
**Multiple microservices in Docker** — Container Apps. You get scaling, ingress, and service discovery without managing Kubernetes.

data.title: Exercise: Pick a Hosting Model
data.description: For each scenario, choose the best Azure compute service and explain why.
steps: Read each scenario below and write down the service you would choose.
Explain your choice in one or two sentences.
Consider cost, management effort, and scalability.
Review your answers against the decision framework.
data.expectedOutcome: You will be able to justify a hosting choice for common application patterns.

data.title: Scenarios
items: A company blog that gets a few hundred views per day.
A file processing service that runs when a user uploads a file to Blob Storage.
A microservices-based ordering system with ten separate services.
A legacy Windows desktop app that needs to be hosted in the cloud.
A REST API with unpredictable traffic that spikes during product launches.

data.title: Start Simple
data.text: When in doubt, start with App Service. It is the easiest to learn, well documented, and covers most common scenarios. You can always migrate to another service later if your needs change.

data.title: Estimate before you build
data.text: Use the Azure Pricing Calculator with realistic request volume, execution duration, and data transfer. A service that looks cheap per execution can be expensive at high volume, and an always-on App Service plan can be cheaper than millions of short function executions. Re-evaluate after you have production telemetry.
Deploying the Same App to Two Hosts

The decision is easier to judge when you see the deployment. Both examples below host the same API; the difference is how much infrastructure the platform manages for you. App Service takes an app and a plan, while Container Apps takes a container image and scales to zero.

data.title: App Service versus Container Apps in Bicep
data.content: The App Service snippet is a plan plus a site; the Container Apps snippet is an environment plus an app that references an image. The second is more moving parts, and it buys scale-to-zero and per-second billing.

data.title: Scale to zero changes the cost model, not just the price
data.text: A scale-to-zero host bills nothing when idle but pays for it with a cold start on the first request after a quiet period. An always-on App Service plan bills whether or not anyone calls it, but never has a cold start. When you compare the two, compare the idle cost and the cold-start budget together — that is the real trade-off, not the headline price.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use App Service for most continuously running web apps and APIs.
Use Functions for event-driven, sporadic, or scheduled workloads.
Use Container Apps when your app runs in Docker or uses microservices.
Use VMs only when you need full control over the operating system.
Start simple and migrate later if your requirements change.
data.takeaway: The best hosting model is the one that fits your workload without adding unnecessary complexity.
